title: Web, data or ML? How I split my time as a 3rd-year CE student
summary: There are too many things to learn. Here is the simple rule I use: build projects that force me to learn the next skill.
html:
I am a 3rd-year Computer Engineering student in Ahmedabad. Like many students, I keep running into the same question: should I focus on web development, data analytics or machine learning? My answer so far is to stop choosing and let projects decide.

Why one track is not enough for me

My own projects already cross these areas:

  • Syntra and HackHub are web platforms (Django, Next.js, Flask).
  • Stock and IPL dashboards are data analytics (Power BI, SQL, Python).
  • OmniDoc AI and the video transcriber use the Gemini API.

Each area makes the others stronger. Web skills help me ship data and AI work as real products. Data skills help me understand what my apps store. AI features make web apps more useful.

The rule I follow

Pick a project that is slightly beyond what I know, and learn only what blocks me.

This avoids two traps:

  1. Tutorial hell. Watching courses without building anything.
  2. Random building. Making projects that never stretch me.

A simple weekly structure

  • Build (most of my time): one active project with a small goal per week
  • Learn on demand: read docs when I am stuck, not before
  • Revise fundamentals (a little every week): DSA, SQL and Python basics, because everything else sits on them
  • Write it down: a short note after each milestone (this blog is part of that)

What I keep from college

University subjects can feel disconnected from projects, but they connect more than I expected. DBMS helped me design the Stocxsim tables. Operating systems and multithreading made sense when I built the JavaFX stock simulator. DSA practice makes me notice slow code.

What I would tell a first-year student

  • Start building early, even tiny things.
  • Put your code on GitHub from day one.
  • Finish projects. One finished, deployed project beats five half-done ones.
  • Learn SQL. It shows up everywhere.

Takeaway

You do not need the perfect roadmap. You need a project that is a little too hard, some patience, and the habit of finishing.

title: How an AI video and voice transcriber works: FFmpeg, FastAPI and Gemini
summary: The pipeline behind my AI Video & Voice Transcriber: extract audio with FFmpeg, send it to Gemini, and return timestamped text to a React UI.
html:
The AI Video & Voice Transcriber turns uploaded video or audio files, or links such as YouTube, into accurate timestamped transcripts. It uses React and TypeScript on the frontend, FastAPI on the backend, FFmpeg for media handling and the Gemini API for transcription. Here is the pipeline in plain steps.

The pipeline

  1. The user uploads a file or pastes a link.
  2. The backend downloads or stores the media.
  3. FFmpeg extracts a small mono audio file.
  4. The audio is sent to Gemini with a clear prompt.
  5. The transcript with timestamps goes back to the frontend.

Why extract audio first

Video files are large and most of the data is pictures you do not need for transcription. A mono, 16 kHz audio file is much smaller and faster to upload.

ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -vn -ac 1 -ar 16000 -b:a 64k audio.mp3
  • -vn drops the video
  • -ac 1 makes it mono
  • -ar 16000 sets a 16 kHz sample rate

A small FastAPI endpoint

@app.post("/transcribe")
async def transcribe(file: UploadFile):
    path = save_temp(file)
    audio = extract_audio(path)       # runs FFmpeg
    text = call_gemini(audio)         # sends audio + prompt
    return {"transcript": text}

Keeping each step in its own function makes it easy to test, and easy to swap one part later.

Prompting matters

Transcription quality depends on the instructions. Ask clearly for:

  • the exact words spoken, without summarising
  • a timestamp at the start of each paragraph
  • a fixed format, so the frontend can parse it

A consistent output format is what lets the React side render clickable timestamps.

Long files

Very long recordings can hit size or time limits. The usual fix is to split the audio into chunks (for example 10 minutes each), transcribe them one by one, and add the chunk's start time to each timestamp when joining.

Things to handle properly

  • Loading states. Transcription takes time, so show progress.
  • Errors. Bad links, unsupported files and API failures should give clear messages.
  • Cleanup. Delete temporary files after processing.
  • API keys. Keep the Gemini key on the server, never in the React code.

Takeaway

An AI feature is mostly normal engineering around one model call: prepare the input, call the model with a clear prompt, and present the output well.

title: From raw IPL data to insights: how I approach a cricket dashboard
summary: A practical workflow for IPL analytics: clean the data, explore it in Python, and present batting and bowling insights in Power BI.
html:
Cricket generates a huge amount of data, and the IPL is a great practice ground for data analytics. My IPL Analytics Dashboard is an interactive Power BI report on matches, team performance and player statistics. This is the workflow I follow for a project like this.

1. Understand the dataset

IPL datasets usually have two main tables:

  • Matches: one row per match (season, teams, venue, toss, winner)
  • Deliveries: one row per ball (batter, bowler, runs, wickets, extras)

Join them using the match ID. Before doing anything else, check row counts, nulls and team names. Teams get renamed over the years (for example, a franchise name change), so standardise them early.

2. Explore in Python

Quick EDA answers "is this data trustworthy?" before you build visuals.

import pandas as pd

matches = pd.read_csv("matches.csv")
print(matches["season"].value_counts().sort_index())
print(matches.isna().sum())

Then try simple questions: does winning the toss help, which venues favour chasing, who scores the most in the powerplay.

3. Define metrics carefully

Cricket metrics are easy to get wrong.

  • Strike rate = runs ÷ legal balls faced × 100. Wides do not count as balls faced.
  • Economy rate = runs conceded ÷ overs bowled. Count overs from legal balls.
  • Batting average needs a rule for not-outs.

In DAX, a strike rate measure looks like this (column names depend on your data):

Strike Rate =
DIVIDE ( SUM ( Deliveries[batsman_runs] ), COUNTROWS ( FILTER ( Deliveries, Deliveries[is_wide] = 0 ) ) ) * 100

4. Design the report

I like one page per question:

  1. Overview: seasons, matches, top teams
  2. Batting: top run scorers, strike rate by phase
  3. Bowling: wickets, economy by phase
  4. Teams and venues: win rates, toss impact

Slicers for season and team let readers explore on their own.

5. Watch out for small samples

A batter with 20 balls faced can show a strike rate of 250. Add a minimum-balls filter so leaderboards stay meaningful.

Takeaway

Good sports analytics is 70 percent data cleaning and metric definitions, and 30 percent charts. Get the definitions right and the visuals become straightforward.

title: Turning 5-minute stock data into a Power BI dashboard
summary: How to model intraday OHLCV data in Power BI, which measures to write, and the mistakes that make stock dashboards misleading.
html:
My Stock Market Analytics Dashboard is a Power BI report built on 5-minute OHLCV data (Open, High, Low, Close, Volume). Intraday data is large and noisy, so how you model it decides whether the dashboard is useful or just busy.

Start with questions

Before touching Power BI, write down what you want to answer:

  • How volatile was the stock today?
  • When does volume peak during the day?
  • How does today compare with the last 10 days?

Every visual should answer one of these. If it does not, remove it.

Clean data first

Intraday files often have gaps, duplicate timestamps or rows outside market hours. I prepare the data in Python (pandas) or Power Query before loading it:

df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=["datetime", "symbol"])
df = df[(df["datetime"].dt.time >= time(9, 15)) & (df["datetime"].dt.time <= time(15, 30))]

NSE trades from 9:15 to 15:30 IST, so anything outside that window is a red flag.

A simple model

  • A Prices fact table (one row per symbol per 5 minutes)
  • A Calendar table for dates
  • A Time table if you want to group by hour or session

Relate Prices to Calendar by date. A proper calendar table makes "last 10 days" and "same day last week" much easier.

Measures worth writing

Day Range = MAX ( Prices[High] ) - MIN ( Prices[Low] )

Total Volume = SUM ( Prices[Volume] )

VWAP =
DIVIDE (
    SUMX ( Prices, ( Prices[High] + Prices[Low] + Prices[Close] ) / 3 * Prices[Volume] ),
    SUM ( Prices[Volume] )
)

Column names depend on your dataset. VWAP (volume weighted average price) is a good one to learn because it shows why you should not just average prices.

Mistakes to avoid

  1. Averaging percentages. Calculate the return from the first open and last close instead.
  2. Too many colours. Use one colour for up and one for down, and keep the rest neutral.
  3. No context. A number without a comparison (yesterday, 10-day average) tells you little.
  4. Ignoring slicer interactions. Test that every visual reacts correctly when you filter by date or symbol.

Takeaway

A good dashboard is a set of answered questions on one page. Clean the data, build a small proper model, and write a few meaningful measures.

title: Building Stocxsim: a paper trading simulator with live market data
summary: How a web paper trading app is put together: live prices, a Socket.IO feed, order handling and a PostgreSQL ledger.
html:
Stocxsim is a web-based paper trading simulator. You trade with virtual money, but the prices come from live NSE/BSE market data through Angel One's SmartAPI. It is built with Flask, Socket.IO, PostgreSQL and Plotly. Here is how the pieces fit together.

The big picture

  1. A backend job fetches live prices from SmartAPI.
  2. The server pushes price updates to the browser over Socket.IO.
  3. The user places a virtual order.
  4. The server checks balance and holdings, records the trade, and updates the portfolio.
  5. Plotly charts show prices and portfolio value.

Why WebSockets instead of polling

If every browser asked the server for new prices every second, the server would be busy answering mostly unchanged data. With Socket.IO the server pushes only when there is something new.

@socketio.on("subscribe")
def subscribe(data):
    join_room(data["symbol"])

def publish_tick(symbol, price):
    socketio.emit("tick", {"symbol": symbol, "price": price}, to=symbol)

Using rooms per symbol means a user only receives updates for the stocks they are watching.

Treat money like a ledger

Even with fake money, the database should behave like a real one. I think of it as two rules:

  • Never edit a balance directly. Record each trade as a row and derive the balance from it.
  • Do the check and the update in one transaction. Otherwise two quick orders could both pass the balance check.
wallet = Wallet.query.with_for_update().get(user_id)  # locks the row
if wallet.balance < cost:
    raise ValueError("Insufficient balance")
wallet.balance -= cost
db.session.add(Trade(user_id=user_id, symbol=symbol, qty=qty, price=price))
db.session.commit()  # lock is released here

with_for_update() locks the wallet row until the transaction finishes, which prevents the double-spend problem.

Keep market data and trading logic apart

The part that talks to SmartAPI can fail (network, rate limits, market closed). The part that handles orders should not depend on it directly. A small price service in the middle makes it easy to test the trading logic with fake prices.

What I like about this project

It touches many real backend topics at once: external APIs, real-time updates, transactions and charts. It is a good way to practise those without risking real money.

Takeaway

For a trading app, correctness of the ledger matters more than any chart. Get the transaction logic right first, then make it look good.

title: How QR code check-in works in a Flask hackathon app
summary: A simple, reliable design for QR check-ins: one secret token per participant, one scan endpoint, and no double check-ins.
html:
HackHub is a Flask-based hackathon management platform with separate admin, faculty and participant portals. One of its most useful features is QR code check-in. This post explains the design in simple terms, so you can build the same thing in any web framework.

The idea

Every participant gets a QR code. At the venue, a volunteer scans it. The server marks that person as present. That is all, but a few details decide whether it works smoothly with 300 people in a queue.

1. Encode a random token, not an ID

Do not put a sequential ID like /checkin/42 in the QR code. Anyone could guess other numbers. Generate a random token for each participant and store it.

import secrets

participant.qr_token = secrets.token_urlsafe(16)

The QR code simply contains that token. It is hard to guess, and you can regenerate it if it leaks.

2. One endpoint, three possible answers

The scan endpoint should be tiny and predictable.

@app.post("/api/checkin")
def checkin():
    token = request.json.get("token", "")
    p = Participant.query.filter_by(qr_token=token).first()

    if p is None:
        return {"status": "invalid"}, 404
    if p.checked_in_at:
        return {"status": "already", "at": p.checked_in_at.isoformat()}, 200

    p.checked_in_at = datetime.utcnow()
    db.session.commit()
    return {"status": "ok", "name": p.name}, 200

The three states (ok, already, invalid) let the scanner screen show a clear green, yellow or red result. The already case matters because people do scan twice.

3. Make it idempotent

If the volunteer's phone has a bad connection and retries the request, the participant should not be checked in twice or get an error. Checking checked_in_at first makes the endpoint safe to call again.

4. Role-based access

Only volunteers and admins should be able to call the endpoint. In HackHub the portals are separate, so the scan page lives in the admin side and is protected by login.

5. Plan for bad Wi-Fi

Event Wi-Fi is usually poor. Keep the scanner page light, show the result instantly, and keep a manual search by name as a fallback.

Takeaway

QR check-in looks like a small feature, but a random token, a three-state response and an idempotent endpoint make it reliable on event day.

title: Building a hackathon platform with Django REST and Next.js
summary: Why Syntra splits into a Django REST Framework API and a Next.js frontend, and the decisions that matter when a hackathon runs on it.
html:
Syntra is a hackathon management platform I'm building. It handles the boring but critical parts of running an event: registrations, teams, check-ins and organiser tools. The backend is Django REST Framework and the frontend is Next.js. This post explains why I split it that way and what I would plan for first if I started again.

Why two separate apps

A hackathon platform has two very different audiences. Participants want a fast, clean site on their phone. Organisers want dense admin screens. Keeping the API separate from the UI means both can use the same rules without duplicating them.

  • Django REST Framework gives me models, validation, permissions and an admin panel with very little code.
  • Next.js gives me routing, server rendering for public pages and a good developer experience for the UI.

The API becomes the single source of truth. If a rule changes (for example, team size limit), it changes in one place.

Model the event first, not the screens

The easiest mistake is to start with pages. I find it better to start with the nouns: Event, Participant, Team, Submission. Once the relationships are clear, the endpoints almost write themselves.

class Team(models.Model):
    event = models.ForeignKey(Event, on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name="teams")
    name = models.CharField(max_length=80)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)

    class Meta:
        unique_together = ("event", "name")

The unique_together line is small, but it removes a whole class of "two teams with the same name" bugs at the database level instead of in the UI.

Permissions are the real feature

For an event tool, who can do what matters more than any chart. Participants can edit their own team. Organisers can see everyone. Volunteers can only check people in. In DRF this maps nicely to permission classes, so each viewset states its rule explicitly instead of hiding it in the frontend.

What I would plan early

  1. Auth and roles before any feature. Adding roles later touches everything.
  2. Pagination and filtering on every list endpoint, since registrations can grow quickly right before the deadline.
  3. A clear error format so the Next.js side can show useful messages.
  4. QR check-in as a first-class flow, not an afterthought. On event day it is the feature people actually use.

Takeaway

Splitting the backend and frontend costs a bit more setup, but it pays back as soon as there is more than one kind of user. If you are building something similar, start with the data model and the permissions, then let the UI follow.
